items.anchor: Nonparametric Filters
items.note: Must read, 15 min. The chapter's one move: drop the Gaussian's fixed form, carry the belief as many numbers (bin probabilities in 4.1–4.2, samples in 4.3), and run the ch. 2 Bayes filter on those numbers.

items.anchor: they approximate posteriors by a finite number of values
items.note: DEFINE: nonparametric means no fixed functional form, not few parameters. With the book's example M = 1,000 (p. 97) a particle set over (x, y, θ) is 3,000 numbers against the EKF's 3 + 9.

items.anchor: As the number of parameters goes to infinity, nonparametric techniques tend to converge uniformly to the correct posterior
items.note: WHY: the guarantee is asymptotic and conditional ('under specific smoothness assumptions'). Everything in 4.3.4 is about finite M, the M your robot actually runs.

items.anchor: they are well-suited to represent complex multimodal beliefs
items.note: ROBOT: the RoboCup field is point symmetric, so after a kidnap the posterior has two modes 180° apart. A KF averages them into the centre circle; a histogram or PF keeps both. LINK: t2.3 (ch. 8, MCL).

items.anchor: these techniques comes at the price of added computational complexity
items.note: COST: a histogram's cell count is the product of bins per axis, and the M a PF needs grows with state dimension (p. 113). This is why the drone's INS stays an EKF (t2.2).

items.anchor: Techniques that can adapt the number of parameters to represent the posterior online are called adaptive
items.note: DEFINE: adaptive = M follows the posterior's complexity; resource-adaptive = M follows the CPU budget. LINK: KLD-sampling in ch. 8 (t2.3) is the adaptive version; this chapter gives no algorithm for it.

items.anchor: Particle filters are often implemented as a resource
items.note: ROBOT: on the quadruped the estimator rate is fixed by the control loop, so M is whatever fits in the budget. CODE: the PF in C4 takes M from the incoming particle array, so it can change between steps.
Must read for 4.1.1–4.1.2, skim 4.1.3–4.1.4. A histogram filter is the Bayes filter with the integral replaced by a sum over bins.
Must read, 10 min. Table 4.1 is two lines: a matrix–vector product and an element-wise product with a normalizer.

items.anchor: When applied to finite spaces, such filters are known as discrete Bayes filters
items.note: DEFINE: one algorithm, two names. Discrete Bayes filter when the state is truly finite (door open or closed, which room); histogram filter when bins approximate a continuous state. Only the second carries an approximation error.

items.anchor: We already encountered a discrete Bayes filter in Chapter 2.4.2
items.note: LINK: t2.1, the door example. Run Table 4.1 on it with K = 2 and you must get the ch. 2 numbers back; a natural first oracle for C1.

items.anchor: occupancy grid mapping algorithms assume that each location in the environment is either occupied or free
items.note: LINK: t2.5 (ch. 9). The tracked robot's costmap is this: one binary filter per cell, written in log odds as Table 4.2.

items.anchor: Table 4.1
items.note: Implement. SHAPES: p_prev (K,), transition T (K, K) with T[k, i] = p(x_k | u, x_i), likelihood (K,). Line 3 is p̄ = T @ p_prev; line 4 is p = η · lik * p̄. CODE: C1 hist_predict, hist_update. COST: line 3 is O(K²) dense; a shift-invariant motion model turns it into a convolution (C1, robust).

items.anchor: Line 3 calculates the prediction, the belief for the new state based on the control alone
items.note: WHY: line 3 is Table 2.1 line 3 with ∫ replaced by Σ; line 4 is Bayes rule. Nothing else changed from ch. 2.

items.anchor: the forward pass of a hidden Markov model
items.note: LINK: the HMM forward algorithm (Rabiner and Juang, cited p. 114). HMM libraries commonly run it in log space; do the same once K is large or the likelihood is sharp (C1, robust).
Must read, 20 min. (4.1)–(4.5) turn a continuous density into Table 4.1's inputs. The only approximations are (4.4) and (4.5).

items.anchor: in two of the resulting bins the probability is so close to zero that they cannot be seen
items.note: PITFALL: the bins of Y in Fig. 4.1 are a fresh grid on Y, filled by pushing points through g. A histogram filter keeps one fixed grid and re-bins every step; that re-binning is where resolution is lost.

Partition: bins disjoint and covering dom(X_t). SHAPES: for book ex. 1, a K_x × K_ẋ grid flattened to K. PITFALL: mass that the motion model pushes past the last bin is lost; C1 must decide (clip or renormalize), and its test checks that mass is conserved.

items.anchor: The histogram of the transformed random variable was computed by passing multiple points from each histogram bin of X through the nonlinear function
items.note: FIGURE: lower right is X and its 10-bin histogram, upper right is g, upper left is Y's true density with its histogram. The caption's last sentence is (4.5) done by sub-bin sampling instead of a centre probe. The lecture redraws 4.1 and 4.3 with the same g.

items.anchor: describes a convex region. These regions together form a partitioning of the state space
items.note: DEFINE: bins are convex and disjoint and together are dom(X_t). Convexity is what keeps the bin mean (4.3) inside its bin.

items.anchor: Through the granularity of the decomposition, we can trade off accuracy and computational efficiency
items.note: COST: cells multiply across axes. Book exercise 2(b) asks which axis (x, y or θ) deserves resolution; the motion model answers it, not the grid.

items.anchor: the posterior becomes a piecewise constant PDF
items.note: DEFINE: within a bin the filter knows nothing more than the bin's total. Everything below follows from this one modelling choice.

Density = bin probability / bin volume. CODE: C1 hist_density. PITFALL: p_k is a probability (sums to 1), p(x) a density (integrates to 1); plotting p_k on a non-uniform grid misleads. TEST: Σ_k p(x̂_k) |x_k| = 1.
Representative state: the bin mean; on a regular grid, the cell centre. CODE: C1 grid centres.

Implement. Likelihood of a bin ≈ likelihood at its centre; exact when p(z | x) is affine across the bin (the average of an affine function is its value at the centre), and (4.7) shows this is the only approximation in the update. PITFALL: a sensor sharper than the bin width misses its peak at every centre. Book ex. 2(c) has Q_meas = 0.01 (σ = 0.1, p. 116), so x-bins coarser than about σ fail here.

Implement. Transition between bins ≈ density at the centres × target-bin volume, then η per source bin. CODE: C1 builds T and normalizes each column so Σ_k T[k, i] = 1; that is the η of (4.10). PITFALL: the deterministic transition of book ex. 2 (p. 115) has no density; add a small R_proc or spread each bin's mass by sub-bin sampling, as Fig. 4.1 does.

items.anchor: a Taylor-approximation analogous to the one used by EKFs
items.note: WHY: the EKF linearizes g once at the mean; the histogram filter freezes the densities at each bin centre, a zeroth-order step per bin. Shrinking the bins shrinks this error; the EKF has no such knob.
Skim, 20 min; derive (4.7) by hand. (4.6) is exact under (4.2); the only approximation is p(z | x) ≈ p(z | x̂) inside a bin.
Derive by hand, five lines. The ≈ in the first line is the histogram filter's only approximation in the measurement update. READING: (4.8)–(4.10) repeat the trick for the transition; skim them.

items.anchor: This expression is an exact description of the desired probability under the piecewise uniform distribution model
items.note: WHY: the exact bin likelihood is the average of p(z | x) over the bin. CODE: C1's robust variant averages p(z | x) over a few points per bin instead of probing the centre.

items.anchor: Note that the normalizer η becomes necessary to ensure that the approximation is a valid probability distribution
items.note: WHY: this η is per source bin i, a distribution over k. As printed, Table 4.1 leaves p̄ unnormalized and line 4's η normalizes (p. 92). CODE: C1 also normalizes the columns of T so p̄ stays a distribution.
Skim. The result is (4.5). The factor |x_k,t| stays unless every bin has the same volume (next sentence).

items.anchor: we can simply omit the factor
items.note: PITFALL: only on a uniform grid. Density trees (4.1.4) or log-spaced range bins have unequal volumes, and dropping |x_k| biases mass toward the small bins ((4.5) multiplies by |x_k|).

items.anchor: do not constitute a probability distribution, since they are not normalized
items.note: PITFALL: Table 4.1 line 3 with (4.5) minus its η gives a p̄ that does not sum to 1; line 4 hides it. Normalize T's columns once and p̄ is a distribution, so a mass check after line 3 catches transition bugs (C1 test).
Skim, 10 min. Static grid, density tree, selective updating, topological vs. metric. Take the ideas; nothing here is implemented in the package.

items.anchor: Dynamic vs. static decomposition
items.note: FIGURE: the same Y as Fig. 4.1 with the same number of bins; the tree puts its bins where the mass is. Not redrawn in the lecture.

items.anchor: Density trees decompose the state space recursively
items.note: DEFINE: resolution follows probability mass. LINK: an octree map (OctoMap) is the mapping cousin used on the quadruped and drone; the density tree returns as a density extractor on p. 105.

items.anchor: Dynamic techniques like density trees can often cut the computation complexity by orders of magnitude
items.note: COST: the book's claim; it gives no numbers. The price is implementation effort and unequal bin volumes (see the |x_k| note on p. 91).

items.anchor: updates only those grid cells whose posterior probability exceeds a user-specified threshold
items.note: PITFALL: cells below threshold are frozen, so a mode that should regrow from low mass (the symmetric twin on the RoboCup field) never can. It is particle deprivation (p. 112) for grids.

items.anchor: They make it possible to use grid decompositions in spaces of three or more dimensions
items.note: ROBOT: (x, y, θ) grid localization in ch. 8 (t2.3) depends on this.

items.anchor: topological representations are often thought of as coarse graph-like representations
items.note: DEFINE: topological = nodes at significant places; metric = a regular grid. The summary (p. 114) calls a decomposition topological when its granularity depends on the environment.

items.anchor: Table 4.2
items.note: Implement. CODE: C2 logodds_update(l_prev, p_inv, p_prior). TEST: equals Table 4.1 on two states with the forward model turned into an inverse one by Bayes rule. PITFALL: the prior term is subtracted on every update, not once; forget it and l drifts under uninformative measurements unless p(x) = 0.5.

items.anchor: Binary Bayes Filters with Static State
items.note: Must read, 25 min. Log odds turn Bayes' product into a sum, and the static state is why Table 4.2 has no prediction step.

items.anchor: a robot estimates a fixed binary quantity in the environment from a sequence of sensor measurements
items.note: ROBOT: one occupancy cell on the tracked robot's map. If the quantity can change (a person walking through the cell), the static assumption breaks and the filter becomes too stubborn; practical mappers (OctoMap) clamp l for this reason; the book does not.
Implement. CODE: C2 prob_to_logodds as log(p) − log1p(−p) (scipy.special.logit). p ∈ {0, 1} gives ±∞; clip p at the inverse sensor model, not inside the filter.

items.anchor: It avoids truncation problems that arise for probabilities close to 0 or 1
items.note: WHY: after many agreeing hits a cell's p is 1 minus something tiny; in floating point 1 − p rounds to 0 and the odds divide by zero. In log odds it is just a large number. Clamping l is common practice (OctoMap), not in the book.

items.anchor: any algorithm that increments and decrements a variable in response to measurements can be interpreted as a Bayes filter in log odds form
items.note: WHY: the hit/miss counters in costmap code are log-odds filters with fixed increments; this sentence tells you what inverse model and prior those increments imply.

items.anchor: This binary Bayes filter uses an inverse measurement model
items.note: DEFINE: p(x | z), state given measurement, the reverse of the p(z | x) used by Table 4.1 and the PF. Table 4.2 needs it plus the prior p(x).

items.anchor: it is easier to implement an inverse than a forward sensor model
items.note: ROBOT: a classifier that outputs P(traversable | image patch) for the tracked robot is an inverse model and plugs into Table 4.2. Its p(x) is the class prior it was trained under, not automatically 0.5.

Implement, but not as written: for large positive l, exp(l) overflows, and the subtraction 1 − 1/(1 + e^l) loses all precision for very negative l. CODE: C2 logodds_to_prob = expit(l), the named trick. TEST: round trip with (4.13) over a wide range of l.
Derive (4.15)–(4.20) by hand. This line swaps the forward model for the inverse one; the p(z_t) it brings in cancels when (4.17) is divided by its ¬x twin (4.18).
Derive by hand. The ratio cancels every term that needs the measurement's marginal. The last factor is the inverse prior odds; it is where Table 4.2's subtraction comes from.
Derive by hand; the second line is Table 4.2 line 2. CODE: C2.

items.anchor: each measurement update involves the addition of the prior
items.note: Wording: the book says 'addition of the prior (in log odds form)'. The term added is log((1 − p(x))/p(x)) = −l0, so in code it is a subtraction of l0, as the second line of (4.20) shows.
Implement: start from l = l0, not 0, unless p(x) = 0.5. TEST (C2): feeding p_inv = p(x) at every step leaves l at l0.

items.anchor: Basic Algorithm
items.note: Must read, 35 min. Table 4.3 has three lines of substance: sample from the motion model, weight by the likelihood, resample. Code it before reading 4.3.2.

items.anchor: by a set of random state samples drawn from this posterior
items.note: WHY: a histogram stores how much mass is in each place; a particle set stores plausible states, and density is how crowded they are (4.23). Particles go where the mass is with no grid to design.

items.anchor: The resulting samples are distributed according to the random variable Y
items.note: FIGURE: same g and Gaussian as Fig. 4.1. Push samples through g and you hold exact samples of Y: no linearization, no bins. ROBOT: skid-steer slip is propagated the same way; you only need to sample it.
SHAPES: the particle set is one (M, n) array; weights are a separate (M,) array. CODE: C4 stores them that way, never as a Python list of ⟨x, w⟩ pairs as Table 4.3 line 6 reads.

items.anchor: a particle is a hypothesis as to what the true world state may be at time
items.note: DEFINE: one full state vector per particle. For the drone that is the whole INS state, which is why the particle count explodes with dimension (p. 113).

items.anchor: the number of particles M is often a large number
items.note: The book's M = 1,000 here and 'M ≥ 100' on p. 98 are orders of magnitude for low-dimensional localization, not rules. Choose your M from the sampling-variance experiment (book ex. 5, T5), not from these.

items.anchor: The particle filter algorithm, a variant of the Bayes filter based on importance sampling
items.note: Implement Table 4.3. SHAPES: X (M, n), w (M,). Line 4: one independent motion-noise draw per particle. Line 5: compute log w, not w. Lines 8–11: draw ∝ w; the book never normalizes w, so normalize before any sampler that assumes Σ w = 1 (Table 4.4). CODE: C4 pf_step, C5 low_variance_resample.

items.anchor: holds only asymptotically for
items.note: PITFALL: for finite M the particles are not samples of the posterior; 'Sampling bias' (p. 112) shows the extreme M = 1. The book's 'negligible for M ≥ 100' is a rule of thumb with no run behind it.
The property a PF aims at, not code. TEST idea (C4): on a linear-Gaussian system the PF's weighted mean and covariance approach the KF's as M grows; the KF from t2.2 is the oracle.

items.anchor: Line 4 generates a hypothetical state
items.note: CODE: needs a sampler for the motion model (ch. 5, t2.4); for the package systems it is g(x, u) plus noise drawn with R_proc. PITFALL: one draw shared by all particles moves the cloud rigidly and the PF degenerates to dead reckoning.

items.anchor: Line 5 calculates for each particle
items.note: DEFINE: importance factor = weight = p(z | x). With a small Q_meas the factors span many orders of magnitude; compute log p(z | x) and normalize with log-sum-exp (C4, robust). TEST: log-space weights equal direct ones wherever the direct ones do not underflow.

items.anchor: These lines implemented what is known as resampling or importance sampling
items.note: Wording: the book calls lines 8–11 'resampling or importance sampling'. Most of the literature calls lines 4–5 importance sampling and lines 8–11 resampling; together, sampling importance resampling (Rubin 1988, cited p. 115). Keep them apart in code.

items.anchor: the resulting sample set usually possesses many duplicates
items.note: WHY: duplicates are the diversity loss of 'Resampling' (p. 108). Line 4 spreads them apart again only if the motion model has noise.
Implement as the no-resampling variant and as the bookkeeping inside (4.36). In log space: log w += log p(z | x). CODE: C4. PITFALL: resetting w to 1 belongs only after a resample (4.36), never here.

items.anchor: The resampling step is a probabilistic implementation of the Darwinian idea of survival of the fittest
items.note: WHY: without resampling the particles stay where the prediction put them and most of the weight sits on a few; resampling moves compute to where the mass is. The cost is diversity (p. 108).
Must read, 25 min. (4.25) and its support condition are the whole theory of the PF update; 4.3.3 only applies them.
Implement as a self-normalized estimator, with (4.27) and (4.28). CODE: C3 is_estimate. TEST: against the exact P_f(A) for a Gaussian target and a Gaussian proposal, computed from the normal CDF.

items.anchor: For this equation to be correct, we need
items.note: PITFALL: f > 0 ⇒ g > 0. A proposal with lighter tails than the target gives rare huge weights, and the estimator's variance can be infinite. In a PF, g is the motion prediction, so an under-sized R_proc is this failure.

items.anchor: Illustration of importance factors in particle filters
items.note: FIGURE: (a) target f; (b) proposal g, samples from g at the bottom; (c) the same samples with bar height f/g. Note g's flat floor across the whole axis: it is what satisfies f > 0 ⇒ g > 0 on the left. In the PF, f is bel(x_t) and g is bel‾(x_t), the prediction. The lecture redraws it.

items.anchor: The distribution that corresponds to the density g is called
items.note: DEFINE: the proposal is where samples come from. The PF's proposal is (4.29), the motion prediction, which ignores z_t. Proposals that use z_t are out of scope (map.md); FastSLAM 2.0 (t2.9) uses one.
Implement (C3). Only the ratio f/g matters, so unnormalized densities are fine once (4.28) normalizes; the PF relies on this with its η.

Implement the self-normalized estimate. TEST (C3): RMS error over seeds falls as 1/√M; fit the slope on a log-log plot against the closed-form value. PITFALL: self-normalized IS is biased at finite M (standard result, not in the book); it is the normalization effect of 'Sampling bias', p. 112.

items.anchor: The constant factor depends on the similarity of f(x) and g(x)
items.note: WHY: the 1/√M rate is fixed; the constant is what you control. A peaky likelihood puts f far from g and makes the constant large, which is why a sharp sensor needs more particles than a vague one.
The PF's proposal: every particle pushed through the motion model. Target over proposal is η p(z | x), derived in (4.34).
Must read, 15 min. On whole paths, target over proposal is η p(z | x). That is why Table 4.3 line 5 is the likelihood and nothing else.
Path particles. Not implemented (memory grows with t). LINK: FastSLAM (t2.9) keeps this path view; smoothing (t2.11) uses the paths on purpose.

items.anchor: Notice the absence of integral signs in this derivation
items.note: WHY: on paths nothing is marginalized, so target and proposal share p(x_0:t−1 | …) exactly and it cancels in (4.34). On x_t alone that cancellation would need the integral over x_t−1.
Derive by hand. Bayes, then two Markov steps; each line uses one assumption from ch. 2.

Derive by hand: target over proposal. PRINT ERROR: on p. 104 the denominator reads z_0:t−1, u_0:t−1 where (4.33) and the numerator have z_1:t−1, u_1:t−1; the same slip is in (4.35). Same quantity; the 0 is a typo.

items.anchor: assuming that our first particle set is obtained by sampling the prior
items.note: PITFALL: the induction base. Initialize particles by sampling p(x_0), not all at the initial guess. Book ex. 2 has Σ_θθ = 10000 (p. 115), i.e. θ effectively uniform on [−π, π) after wrap().

items.anchor: The constant η plays no role since the resampling takes place with
items.note: CODE: so the likelihood never needs its Gaussian normalizer, provided the normalizer is the same for every particle. A per-particle Q_meas (range-dependent noise) must keep its log-determinant term.

items.anchor: The algorithm in Table 4.4 follows now from the simple observation
items.note: PRINT ERROR: 'Table 4.4' should read Table 4.3 (the particle filter). Table 4.4 is the low-variance sampler on p. 110.

items.anchor: As we will argue below, this derivation is only correct for
items.note: WHY: the η in resampling is a sum over the finite particle set, not the true normalizer. 'Sampling bias' on p. 112 is the 'below'.

items.anchor: Density Extraction
items.note: Skim, 10 min. Mean, Gaussian, k-means, histogram, kernel density: choose by what the consumer (controller, planner, another robot) needs.

items.anchor: the mean of the particles provides enough information to control the robot
items.note: ROBOT: only for a unimodal cloud. On the RoboCup field's symmetric posterior the mean sits between the two modes, where no particle is. CODE: C6 reports the weighted mean and covariance, so a bimodal cloud at least shows a large Σ.

items.anchor: the space complexity is exponential in the number of dimensions
items.note: COST: the histogram curse again. Fine for 1-D readouts and for the (x, y) marginal of a pose PF.

items.anchor: Kernel density estimation is another way of converting a particle set into a
items.note: DEFINE: one kernel per particle, density = their mixture. COST: O(M) per query (this page). Used for the lecture's figures (the Fig. 4.6 redraw), not inside the filter.

items.anchor: Sampling Variance
items.note: Must read, 15 min. The PF's output is itself a random variable; Fig. 4.6 shows its spread at M = 25 and M = 250.

items.anchor: Different ways of extracting densities from particles
items.note: FIGURE: (a) samples and true density, (b) Gaussian fit, (c) histogram of weights, (d) kernel density. Same Y as Figs. 4.1 and 4.3.

items.anchor: Variance due to random sampling
items.note: FIGURE: each row is one random experiment; left column 25 samples, right 250 (caption). Read down a column: the spread between rows is the sampling variance. SESSION: a candidate card with M and seed as controls.

items.anchor: Variability due to random sampling is called the variance of the
items.note: DEFINE: run-to-run spread of the estimate, not the spread of the particles. Two identical robots (next paragraph) end up with different beliefs.

items.anchor: Fortunately, the sampling variance decreases with the number of samples
items.note: TEST: the 1/√M law of (4.28). Over many seeds the RMS error at 4M should be about half that at M (C3).

items.anchor: Resampling
items.note: Must read, 30 min. Resampling loses diversity. Two fixes: resample less often ((4.36) with a weight-variance trigger) and resample with lower variance (Table 4.4).

items.anchor: it will be useful to consider the extreme case, which is that of a robot whose state does not change
items.note: ROBOT: the quadruped standing at its dock, the drone hovering. TEST/SESSION: Table 4.3 with no motion noise and no sensor; count unique particles over time until one remains.

items.anchor: M identical copies of a single particle will survive
items.note: WHY: resampling is a random walk on the particle counts with an absorbing state; with no fresh randomness from line 4 it ends there. To an observer the robot looks certain with no sensor at all.

items.anchor: Even though the variance of the particle set itself decreases, the variance of the particle set as an estimator of the true belief increases
items.note: PITFALL: a tight cloud is not a confident filter. Check consistency with NEES as in t2.2; a collapsed cloud sits far above the band.

items.anchor: When the robot stops, resampling should be suspended
items.note: ROBOT: gate resampling (and, as the book says, measurement updates) on odometry. The tracked robot's chassis vibrates when idle and reports small odometry, so gate on a threshold, not on zero.
Implement. In log space: log w ← 0 after a resample, log w += log p(z | x) otherwise. CODE: C4 pf_step with a resampling trigger.

items.anchor: A standard approach to determining whether or not resampling should be performed is to measure the variance of the importance weights
items.note: CODE: C4 uses N_eff = 1/Σ w̃² on normalized weights. For normalized weights N_eff = M / (1 + M² Var(w̃)), a monotone function of the variance the book names. A threshold of N_eff < M/2 is common practice, not from the book.

items.anchor: the selection involves a sequential stochastic process
items.note: DEFINE: one random number, M evenly spaced pointers. The PF literature calls this systematic resampling.

items.anchor: Low variance resampling for the particle filter
items.note: Implement Table 4.4. It assumes normalized weights: r ∈ [0, 1/M), pointers U up to 1, so c must reach 1; the unnormalized w of Table 4.3 breaks it. The text layer renders M⁻¹ as 'M −1'; read 1/M. CODE: C5 low_variance_resample via np.searchsorted on the cumulative sum. PITFALL: round-off leaves cumsum[-1] just below 1; set it to 1 or the last pointer runs off the end.
Implement as searchsorted(cumsum(w), U). TEST (C5): over many runs the mean copy count of particle i is M w_i, and with equal weights the output set equals the input (p. 111).

items.anchor: Principle of the low variance resampling procedure
items.note: FIGURE: weights laid end to end on [0, 1], a comb of M teeth spaced 1/M with offset r. A particle of weight w gets ⌊Mw⌋ or ⌈Mw⌉ copies (a standard property of systematic resampling, not stated in the book). The lecture redraws it.

items.anchor: if all the samples have the same importance factors, the resulting sample set
items.note: TEST: equal weights in, identical set out. Multinomial resampling fails this test, which is the diversity argument in one line.

items.anchor: the low-variance sampler has a complexity of O(M)
items.note: COST: O(M) because the pointers arrive sorted, so one sweep of the cumulative sum serves all of them. Independent draws need a binary search each, O(M log M) as the book says.

items.anchor: Another popular option is stratified sampling
items.note: DEFINE: the book's stratified sampling groups particles into subsets and allocates draws by subset weight. 'Stratified resampling' in the PF literature is different: one uniform per interval [(m−1)/M, m/M). C5 implements the latter as a variant.

items.anchor: tends to perform well when a robot tracks multiple, distinct hypotheses
items.note: ROBOT: on the symmetric RoboCup field, one stratum per mode keeps the twin mode alive until a landmark breaks the tie, instead of a few unlucky draws killing it.

items.anchor: Sampling Bias
items.note: Must read, 10 min. Normalization inside resampling costs one degree of freedom; at M = 1 it costs all of them. Book exercise 3 asks for M = 2.

items.anchor: regardless of its importance factor
items.note: WHY: with one particle, line 9 picks it with probability 1 whatever z says (4.38). The PF becomes dead reckoning, sampling p(x_t | u_1:t).

Derive by hand, then do book exercise 3 (M = 2). EXERCISE: the package works ex. 3 exactly on a two-state example (T2.4, session Fig 2.3e); lecture Fig L10 is the Monte Carlo version on a continuous state.

items.anchor: but after normalization they reside in a space of dimension
items.note: WHY: the same finite-M bias as self-normalized importance sampling (4.28), stated as lost degrees of freedom. It fades as M grows but never reaches zero.

items.anchor: Particle Deprivation
items.note: Must read, 10 min. No particle near the truth means the filter cannot recover. Random injection is the last resort; ch. 8 has the real fixes.

items.anchor: an unlucky series of random numbers can wipe out all particles near the true state
items.note: ROBOT: a robot picked up and moved during a RoboCup match is the deliberate version (kidnapping). SESSION: count steps until no particle lies within a radius of the true pose.

items.anchor: Eventually we will generate an estimate that is arbitrarily incorrect
items.note: WHY: a per-step failure probability above zero makes eventual failure certain over an unbounded run. On a long field test this is not theoretical.
